newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE- Bonn no longer a quiet town on the Rhine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- Bonn no longer a quiet town on the Rhine.

text.p: Germany's growing role on the world stage is causing a small problem at the Foreign Ministry -- the heavy flow of international visitors keep exhausting the budget for biscuits and coffee.

Last year's two million mark ($1.2 million) snacks budget for visiting dignitaries ran out in October. The way things are going this year, the budget, although boosted by an extra 200,000 marks, will also be gobbled up long before Christmas.
The empty biscuit tin is a small, yet telling, indicator of Bonn's growing influence six years after the country reunited.
Long an economic powerhouse, Germany has quietly shed much of its reluctance to stand in the forefront and has become an important political centre of gravity in central Europe.
The number and importance of a steady stream of visitors to Bonn is one reflection of the country's enhanced standing.
"Bonn is one of the cities with the most official visitors in the world," Chancellor Helmut Kohl sometimes reminds his fellow Germans.

Not only have Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin passed through Bonn, a quiet little town on the Rhine, but the city of 300,000 has also been an important destination for a wide array of international visitors.
John Major, Jacques Chirac, Romano Prodi, Jose Maria Aznar, Benjamin Netanyahu and Yasser Arafat were all here recently.

And so were Toomas Hendrik Ilves, Estonia's foreign minister, and Akis Tsochatzopoulous, Greece's defence minister. Brazil's vice president Marco Maciel just spent a week in Bonn and the prime ministers of the Maldives and Tanzania are expected soon.
FOREIGN LEADERS CONVERGE ON BONN
There were 106 visits to Bonn from government heads and foreign ministers in 1996, more than triple the number of visiting leaders a decade earlier.

Hardly a week goes by without a high-ranking foreign visitor keeping protocol officers, police and journalists in perpetual motion. Both U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind were in town in February.

"There are many objective reasons for this," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann. "Germany is the most populous country and has more neighbouring countries than any other country in Europe after Russia. Also, Germany is economically the most powerful country in Europe."

The United States had long nudged Germany to take on a greater world role, but many western European countries with long memories of two world wars this century had a harder time embracing any greater German role.

"Germany has a major role to play in world affairs and a strong role in Europe," Clinton said in Berlin in 1994. "It's not even an option to talk about a world in which Germany doesn't play a leadership role."
GERMAN INFLUENCE GROWS

Whereas foreign leaders from parts of Europe and the developing world once came to the West German capital city looking for financial aid, they now come to Bonn looking to win all kinds of influence with Kohl.

Kohl is at the heart of the European Union's drive to create a single European currency by 1999. He is also seen by many Eastern European countries as their key advocate to back their claims to join the EU and NATO.
Despite tight budget constraints, Germany nevertheless contributed 17 billion marks ($10 billion) in foreign aid last year, double the amount of 10 years earlier.

"Even though the German population has not accepted the fact, there is no doubt about Germany now being a major power," said Karl Kamp, an analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation, a conservative public policy think tank near Bonn.
"Whether you like it or not, Germany is a country that you have to address if you want to express your views on a number of important issues such as NATO enlargement and European integration."
With a population of more than 81 million and a gross domestic product of three trillion marks, Germany trails only the United States and Japan in economic might.

Germany has become an important conduit between Moscow and Washington. Kohl, who spent a much-publicised afternoon in the sauna with Yeltsin two years ago, was the first foreign leader to visit him after his heart operation last year and the two have met nine times in the last four years.

"We are wearing bigger shoes now, but most of the 80 million people in Germany haven't even noticed the change," said one German diplomat. "But the shoes have even grown larger than our feet. Sometimes, too much is expected of us."
MILITARY MISSIONS MARK TURNING-POINT

An important moment in Germany's transformation came in 1995 when parliament dropped a self-imposed ban on sending its military abroad. It now has 3,300 combat troops to Bosnia supporting the U.N.-sponsored SFOR mission.
The mission would have been unthinkable only a few years earlier because of lingering worries about the country's ignominous militaristic past.
But the peacekeeping efforts have been widely applauded both within Germany and overseas, particularly in Washington and at the United Nations in New York.

"Nothing made American politicians happier since German unification than the decision to send Bundeswehr units to Bosnia," wrote Gerald Livingston, director for German studies at Johns Hopkins University, in the newsweekly Der Spiegel.
"American foreign policy makers, in contrast to the political class in France and most European countries, have no fear of a stronger, more confident Germany," he added.
"In contrast to Germany's European neighbours, the United States welcomes the expansion of German influence in Eastern and Southeastern Europe."

Some foreign diplomats in Bonn believe the glut of overseas visitors reflects not only a more active German foreign policy but also shows Germany has still to decide the areas in which it wants to expand its influence following unification.
"Germany has its fingers in a lot of pies. It will have to set some priorities over the next few years," one diplomat said.
But first they will have to find a bigger cookie jar.
